title: Proximity and position sensors: inductive, capacitive, photoelectric, NPN and PNP
goals: Pick inductive, capacitive, photoelectric or magnetic sensing for a target and a distance
Work out a safe sensing distance from Sn, the assured-distance margin and the target's metal
Wire a PNP or NPN sensor to a PLC input that matches it, and say what a meter should read
Check a sensor is fast enough for gear teeth or parts going past
Split a 'sensor works but the PLC doesn't see it' fault with one measurement
summary:
A **proximity sensor** detects a target without touching it and switches an output on or off.

**Inductive**: a coil's magnetic field; **metal only**. The rated distance **Sn** is for a mild-steel plate. Design within the **assured distance**, $0.81 \times S_n$, and multiply by the metal's **correction factor** from the datasheet (roughly: stainless 0.7, brass 0.5, aluminium 0.4, copper 0.3). **Flush** (shielded) types can sit in metal; **non-flush** reach further but need clear space round the face.

**Capacitive**: sees anything that is not air: plastic, wood, grain, water, even through a plastic tank wall. Set its sensitivity for the job; build-up and condensation fool it.

**Photoelectric**: a light beam. **Through-beam** (separate sender and receiver): longest range, most reliable. **Retro-reflective** (bounces off a reflector): shiny parts can fool it, so use a **polarised** type. **Diffuse** (bounces off the target): shortest range, depends on colour.

**Magnetic** (reed or Hall) sensors clip to air cylinders and see the magnet in the piston.

**Wiring** (3-wire DC): **brown +24 V, blue 0 V, black output** (white: a second, opposite output). **PNP** switches the black wire to **+24 V**: the PLC input sits between black and 0 V. **NPN** switches black to **0 V**: the load sits between +24 V and black. UK and European kit is mostly PNP. The input card must match: a PNP sensor needs an input whose common goes to 0 V. The wrong pairing never turns on, while the sensor's own LED still lights.

**Meter checks**, black to blue with the target present: PNP about 24 V, NPN about 0 V.

**Speed**: a gear with N teeth at n rpm gives $\frac{Nn}{60}$ pulses a second. That must be below the sensor's maximum switching frequency. **Hysteresis** (it switches off a little further out than it switches on) stops chatter at the edge.

**Fault finding**: sensor LED on but PLC input off? Measure from the PLC input terminal to 0 V (24 V DC, measuring only, if authorised). 24 V there: the input or its common. None: the cable, terminals or fuse.

bench.task: Wire a 24 V DC PNP inductive sensor to a bench power supply (current limit about 100 mA) with a 24 V relay coil or LED indicator drawing under 50 mA as its load, then measure it. Low voltage only; no PLC needed.
check: Brown to +24 V, blue to 0 V, the load from black to 0 V
Bring a steel spanner up to the face: find where it switches on and where it switches off (the hysteresis)
Try an aluminium or brass part: how much closer must it be?
With the target there, measure black to blue (about 24 V), then take it away (about 0 V)

cards.q: An inductive sensor rated 8 mm reliably detects a **steel** bracket 6 mm away. The bracket is changed to **aluminium**, still 6 mm away. What happens?
options: Nothing changes: both metals are seen the same
It will probably stop seeing it: aluminium is seen less far
It sees it further away: aluminium conducts better
It sees it only when the bracket is moving
cards.why: The rated distance is for mild steel. Aluminium's correction factor is typically about 0.4, so this sensor reliably sees it only to about 2.6 mm. Better conductivity does not help: an inductive sensor senses the losses in the target, and aluminium makes fewer.

cards.title: Four ways to sense without touching
cards.body:
A **proximity sensor** switches an output when a target is near, without touching it. Choose by what the target is made of and how far away it is:

- **Inductive**: a magnetic field; sees **metal only**, up to a few tens of millimetres at most.
- **Capacitive**: an electric field; sees **almost anything** that is not air, even through a plastic wall.
- **Photoelectric**: a **light beam**; sees most things, from millimetres to many metres.
- **Magnetic** (reed or Hall): sees a **magnet**, such as the one in an air cylinder's piston.

A mechanical **limit switch** does touch: it is simple and can be seen working, and safety-rated ones force their contacts open.

cards.q: Match each job with the sensor for it.
pairs: Grain level, through a plastic hopper wall
Cardboard boxes across a 2 m conveyor
The piston inside an aluminium air cylinder
cards.why: Inductive for metal close up; capacitive for non-metals and through non-metal walls; photoelectric for distance; magnetic to see a piston magnet through the cylinder's aluminium body.

cards.title: Inductive: metal, and how far
cards.body:
A coil in the face makes a changing magnetic field. Metal in the field soaks up energy (eddy currents), and the sensor switches.

The datasheet's **rated distance, Sn**, is measured on a **mild-steel plate**. Two things shrink it:
- Rely only on the **assured distance**: $0.81 \times S_n$, which allows for temperature and batch spread.
- Other metals are seen less far: multiply by the **correction factor**, roughly stainless 0.7, brass 0.5, aluminium 0.4, copper 0.3. Check the datasheet.

**Flush** (shielded) sensors can sit flush in a metal bracket. **Non-flush** ones reach further but need clear space round the face.
cards.more: Picture the steel plate the datasheet was measured with as the 'full marks' target. Anything else scores less. Suppose an M18 non-flush sensor has Sn = 8 mm. First take off the safety margin: 8 × 0.81 = 6.5 mm is as far as you should count on, even for mild steel. Then for aluminium, × 0.4: 6.5 × 0.4 ≈ 2.6 mm. So a bracket that worked at 6 mm in steel needs to be under about 2.6 mm in aluminium. Some sensors, sold as 'factor 1', see all metals at the same distance: worth it when targets vary.

cards.q: An inductive sensor's rated distance is Sn = {sn} mm. Keeping to the assured distance, $0.81 \times S_n$, how far away can you rely on it seeing a **mild-steel** target, in mm?
cards.why: Mild steel is what Sn is measured on, so its factor is 1: only the 81% margin comes off.
cards.hint: Mild steel needs no correction factor. Just take 81% of Sn.

cards.title: Capacitive: almost anything
cards.body:
A capacitive sensor's face is one plate of a capacitor; the surroundings are the other. Anything with a **dielectric constant** above air's (it stores electric field better than air) changes the capacitance: plastic, wood, grain, powder and, strongly, **water**.

So it can see a **liquid through a plastic tank wall**, or granules in a hopper.

The price: it sees almost everything, so you set its **sensitivity** (a small screw or teach button) for each job. **Build-up**, condensation or a wet film on the face can hold it on, and a metal wall blocks it completely.

cards.q: A capacitive sensor on the outside of a plastic tank switches when the liquid reaches it. Lately it stays on even with the tank empty. What is most likely?
options: A film of liquid or condensation on the wall at the sensor
The liquid is not metal, so the sensor cannot see it
The sensor is PNP and the PLC input expects NPN
The tank wall is too thin to sense through
cards.why: A capacitive sensor sees any film of material in front of it. A coating left behind looks just like a full tank. Not metal is fine: that is the point of a capacitive sensor. A PNP/NPN mismatch would stop it ever reading on, not hold it on.

cards.title: Photoelectric: three layouts
cards.body:
- **Through-beam**: a sender and a separate receiver face each other; the target breaks the beam. Longest range and most reliable, but two parts to mount and wire.
- **Retro-reflective**: sender and receiver in one body, bouncing the beam off a **reflector**. One part to wire. A **shiny** target can bounce the beam back and fool it: a **polarised** type, with a corner-cube reflector, ignores such reflections.
- **Diffuse**: the beam bounces off the **target** itself. Simplest to fit, shortest range, and dark or shiny targets change the range. **Background suppression** types ignore anything beyond a set distance.

**Light-on** or **dark-on** sets whether the output is on when light is received or when it is blocked.

cards.q: A retro-reflective sensor keeps missing shiny stainless trays passing between it and its reflector. What fixes it?
options: A bigger reflector, so that more of the light returns
Setting the sensor to dark-on instead of light-on
A diffuse sensor aimed at the trays instead
A polarised retro-reflective sensor, or a through-beam pair
cards.why: The shiny tray reflects the beam straight back, so the sensor thinks the beam is still unbroken. A polarised sensor accepts only light whose polarisation the corner-cube reflector has turned; a mirror-like surface returns it unturned. A bigger reflector changes nothing, and a diffuse sensor struggles with shiny targets too.

cards.title: Wiring: PNP and NPN
cards.body:
Three-wire DC sensors: **brown +24 V, blue 0 V, black the output** (white: a second, opposite output on 4-wire types).

The sensor is a switch. **PNP** switches the black wire to **+24 V**; **NPN** switches it to **0 V**:

```
PNP:  +24V --[sensor]-- black --[PLC input]-- 0V
NPN:  +24V --[ load ]-- black --[sensor]----- 0V
```

UK and European kit is mostly **PNP**; Japanese and some US kit, NPN. The PLC input must match: a PNP sensor needs an input whose **common goes to 0 V**, so current flows in from the sensor. The wrong pairing never turns on, while the sensor's own LED still lights.
cards.more:
Ask which side of the load the switch is on. PNP puts the switch on the +24 V side, like a light switch in the live: when it closes, the black wire rises to 24 V and current flows through the PLC input down to 0 V. NPN puts the switch on the 0 V side: when it closes, the black wire drops to 0 V and current flows from +24 V through the load into the sensor.

So a meter from black to blue (0 V) with the target present reads about **24 V for PNP** and about **0 V for NPN**. With no target: 0 V for PNP; for NPN, whatever the load pulls it to, often 24 V.

cards.q: A PNP sensor is on (its target is there). What does a meter read from its black wire to its blue wire?
options: About 0 V
About 12 V
About 24 V
It depends on the target's metal
cards.why: PNP switches black to +24 V, and blue is 0 V. An NPN sensor, switched on, would read about 0 V: its output is pulled down to the blue wire.

cards.title: Fast enough? Switching frequency
cards.body:
Every sensor has a **maximum switching frequency** on its datasheet: how many on-off cycles a second it can follow. Past it, pulses merge and counts go missing.

Counting gear teeth: a gear with **N** teeth turning at **n** rpm passes $\frac{Nn}{60}$ teeth a second (n ÷ 60 is revolutions per second).

A 30-tooth gear at 1200 rpm: $\frac{30 \times 1200}{60} = 600$ pulses a second. A sensor rated 500 Hz would miss some. So would a PLC input with a slow filter: fast counts need a high-speed counter input.

**Hysteresis** is different: the sensor switches off a little further out than it switched on, so a target sitting at the edge does not chatter.

cards.q: A {t}-tooth steel gear turns at {n} rpm past an inductive sensor. How many pulses a second does the sensor see, in Hz?
cards.why: Teeth per revolution × revolutions per second. Forgetting the ÷ 60 gives pulses a minute, 60 times too many.
cards.hint: How many revolutions a second is {n} rpm?

cards.q: An inductive sensor has Sn = {sn} mm. The target is **brass** (correction factor 0.5). Keeping to the assured distance, how far away can you rely on it, in mm?
cards.why: Both reductions apply: the 81% margin for any target, then the brass factor.
cards.hint: Two multiplications: the margin, then the metal.

cards.q: A replacement sensor turns out to be **NPN**. The PLC input card is wired for PNP sensors, with its common at 0 V. What happens?
options: It works back to front: on when the target is away
The input never turns on
It works normally: PNP and NPN only differ in name
The PLC input stays on all the time
cards.why: Current needs a voltage across the input. With the common at 0 V, only a +24 V signal drives current through it, and an NPN sensor never gives one. The sensor's LED still lights, which is what makes this confusing on a breakdown.

cards.q: This wiring list is for a **PNP** sensor into an S7-1200 input. One line is wrong. Which?
cards.why: A PNP sensor puts +24 V on the input, so the input's common must go back to 0 V for current to flow. With 1M at +24 V, both sides of the input sit at 24 V when the sensor is on: no current, and the input never turns on. (1M to +24 V is how you would wire NPN sensors.)

cards.q: A sensor's LED lights when the target is there, but the PLC input stays off. What is the best next check?
options: Measure from the PLC input terminal to 0 V, target present
Replace the sensor, since it may be switching weakly
Move the sensor closer to the target and try again
Change the PLC input card for a new one
cards.why: The LED shows the sensor's output switched, so the fault lies between the sensor and the PLC. Measure from the input terminal to 0 V: 24 V there means the input card or its common (measure 1M to 0 V next); 0 V means the cable, a terminal or a fuse. (Live testing: 24 V DC control, measuring only, with GS38 probes, and only if you are authorised. Keep clear of the 400 V parts, and make sure the machine is safe to start if the fault clears.)

cards.q: A sensor's maximum switching frequency is {f} Hz. It counts the teeth of a {t}-tooth gear. What is the fastest the gear can turn before counts go missing, in rpm?
cards.why: Rearrange $f = \frac{Nn}{60}$ for n. In practice stay well below it: the rating assumes an ideal target.
cards.hint: Pulses a second ÷ teeth = revolutions a second. Then × 60.

cards.q: Why is a through-beam pair the most reliable choice for boxes that may be dirty, shiny or any colour?
options: Through-beam sensors use a laser, which is brighter
It needs only one part to mount and wire
It detects metal targets as well as cardboard
It only has to block the beam, whatever its colour or shine
cards.why: A diffuse sensor depends on light coming back off the box, so colour and finish matter. A retro-reflective one can be fooled by shine. Through-beam only asks: is the beam blocked? The cost is two parts to mount and wire.

cards.q: An inductive sensor has Sn = {sn} mm. The target is aluminium (factor 0.4). Keeping to the assured distance, how close must the target come, in mm?
cards.why: Margin, then metal: 0.81 × 0.4 is about a third of Sn.

cards.q: A PLC input behaves like a {r} kΩ resistor. What current does a PNP sensor send into it at 24 V, in mA?
cards.work: $I = \frac{ V }{ R } = \frac{24}{{{r}}} = {answer:2}$ mA (volts ÷ kΩ gives mA)
cards.why: Ohm's law. A few milliamps, far below the 100 mA or more a sensor output can switch, so one sensor can drive an input easily.
cards.hint: Which law links volts, ohms and amps?

cards.q: Plastic bottles full of water pass along a conveyor. Which sensor will **not** see a bottle?
options: Capacitive
Through-beam photoelectric
Inductive
Diffuse photoelectric
cards.why: Inductive sensors need metal. The water makes the bottle easy for a capacitive sensor, and either photoelectric type can see it, though a clear bottle may need a sensor made for transparent objects.

cards.q: An inductive sensor was set up near the edge of its range on a **steel** part. The part is changed to **brass**. What do you expect?
options: It sees it further away than steel
It may miss the part
No change: it sees any metal equally
It sees it only while the part moves
cards.why: Brass's correction factor is about 0.5. Near the edge for steel means well out of range for brass. Move the sensor closer, or use a 'factor 1' sensor that sees all metals at the same distance.

cards.q: An **NPN** sensor is on (its target is there). What does a meter read from its black wire to its blue wire?
options: About 0 V
About 24 V
About 12 V
Nothing: an NPN sensor has no output
cards.why: Blue is 0 V and the NPN output is switched to it, so the two are at the same voltage. Measure black to brown instead and you see about 24 V across the load's side. A PNP sensor would read about 24 V black to blue.

cards.q: Match each wire of a DC proximity sensor with what it is.
pairs: A second, opposite output (on many 4-wire types)
cards.why: The IEC colours for DC sensors. The white output is on when the black one is off, handy when you need both.
